newsitem.title: UK: Africa's share of world rubber trade is seen higher.
newsitem.headline: Africa's share of world rubber trade is seen higher.

text.p: Africa is set to expand its share of the world natural rubber market in coming decades as exports from Asia are predicted to stagnate, according to African planters and Western experts at a conference in Liverpool.
African officials agreed that African output was still small compared with that from heavyweights Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia, the three big players that have long dominated the rubber scene.
But Africa offers the best growth prospects in terms of future supply, they said.
Africa's share of world production would grow to 4.7 percent in 2000 and 7.6 percent in 2020 from about 4.0 percent now, several Western experts predicted.

But the share from Thailand, the largest grower, is seen falling from 29 percent in 2000 to 19 percent in 2010, compared with 24 percent in 1990, said Hidde Smit, managing director Amsterdam-based Economic and Social Institute.
"The future of rubber is in Africa," a Nigerian industry official said. "We have the land mass, conducive climate, low costs and abundant labour supply."
An African rubber scientist added that "the same clone that yields 1,200 kg per hectare a year in southeast Asia will give 1,500 kg in Africa without additional fertiliser".
Economists at the international experts' forum said rubber could face a severe supply shortage in the decade as stagnant production from southeast Asia is not matched with a sharp increase elsewhere.
Chinese output is already approaching its peak, India's planting industry has problems and there is a lack of investments in plantations in smaller Asian producers.

Malaysia was once the world's largest rubber producer. But rapid industrialisation has caused a shortage of rubber tappers. It also made land and capital relatively expensive for continued rubber production.
Also, more natural rubber is consumed domestically in southeast Asia, leaving less for the world market, said Prachaya Jumpasut, chief economist at the 21-member International Rubber Study Group.

Mapri Kpolo, executive secretary of the Professional Association of Natural Rubber of Africa (ARA), said at the forum that output from nine major African producing countries could reach 324,000 tonnes in 1998 from 300,000 in 1997.
Several governments have privatised the rubber sector and old rubber trees have been replanted with higher-yielding clones.
ANRA is also formulating new standards for African rubber which could improve quality and remove the current five to 20 percent origin discounts to southeast Asian rubber.

The so-called Standard African Rubber is expected to hit the market by end-1998. But despite inherent advantages, the African industry is still beset by lack of development funds for the core smallholding sector and political instability in some countries.
"The only problem is the political instability," said one Nigerian estate manager. "No multinational firms want to invest if there is no stability." --London Newsroom +44 171 542 4985
